title: The Desk in the Old Executive Office Building: the Marine, the Enterprise, and the Record That Copied Itself
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: San Antonio, the birth on the seventh of October
stops.date_confidence: attested: date and city agree across Wikipedia, Britannica, and North's own memoir
stops.campa: Oliver Laurence North is born on the seventh of October in San Antonio, Texas, the third of four children in a family that will not stay. The city keeps no further claim on him: no school, no street, no first job. What the record holds of this place is the date and the name, and both will be read out four decades later in a federal courtroom and on live television, at the head of an indictment and at the head of a defense. The rest of the boyhood happens six hundred miles northeast, in another state entirely.
suggested_refs: Birth records and the biographical sketch circulated to the joint congressional committees, 1987
sources: Oliver North with William Novak, Under Fire: An American Story (1991)

stops.name: Philmont, the mill town on the Agawamuck
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the family's residence at Philmont spans roughly 1944 to 1961 and the 1961 graduation from Ockawamick Central is attested; the year given here marks the period, not a documented event
stops.campa: The family settles in Philmont, a mill town in Columbia County where the Agawamuck runs through the middle of the village and the woolen mills are already closing. North grows up here, works summer jobs, attends Ockawamick Central High School, and graduates in 1961. This is the origin he will tell: small town, churchgoing family, scouting, the Hudson Valley rather than the Texas one. Every profile written after 1986 opens here rather than in San Antonio, and takes the account from him.
suggested_refs: Ockawamick Central High School records; local Columbia County press profiles of the Iran-Contra years

stops.name: Brockport, two years before the appointment
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the two-year attendance and the 1963 Academy appointment; the month is conventional. The research pool tagged this [R]; the tag is corrected to [A], since Wikipedia states the attendance plainly rather than reconstructing it
stops.campa: He enrolls at the State University of New York at Brockport in 1961 and stays two years. The coursework, the grades, and the reason he leaves are absent from the reachable record; the enrolment registers are not published. What is documented is the exit. He seeks and receives an appointment to the United States Naval Academy and leaves for Annapolis in 1963. Iran-Contra retrospectives skip this town. After it he holds a rank, and a superior, for the rest of his working life.
suggested_refs: SUNY Brockport enrollment records for 1961-1963, not published

stops.name: Annapolis, Bancroft Hall and the delayed commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of entry (1963) and the year of commissioning (1968); the induction day is conventional
stops.campa: North enters the Naval Academy in 1963 and lives in Bancroft Hall with a class that will scatter across Vietnam-era commands. The curriculum here is chain of command, lawful order, and the officer's obligation to the man above him. Injuries from an automobile accident delay his commissioning by roughly a year, so that he takes his second lieutenant's bars in 1968. In 1987, at the witness table, he will answer the committees in the vocabulary he is taught in this building.
suggested_refs: United States Naval Academy alumni records, class of 1968

stops.name: Camp Barrett, The Basic School
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month conventional. Coordinates corrected: the research pool placed this at Quantico main side (38.5223, -77.2955); The Basic School sits at Camp Barrett, roughly four kilometres west-southwest
stops.campa: Commissioned a second lieutenant of Marines in 1968, North reports to The Basic School at Camp Barrett, the infantry-officer pipeline through which every Marine lieutenant of the era passes on the way to the war. He learns the platoon: fire and maneuver, the map, the radio, the casualty. He will return to Quantico as an instructor within two years, teaching the same syllabus to men bound for the same province. The war is at its height and the school is running lieutenants through at speed.
suggested_refs: The Basic School course records, Camp Barrett, Marine Corps Base Quantico
sources: US Marine Corps service record summaries cited in Iran-Contra biographies

stops.name: Da Nang, the gate into the war
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the arrival is attested by North's memoir and standard unit deployment timelines; the exact date is not independently corroborated
stops.campa: North comes into the war through Da Nang, the fishing port turned airbase where the logistics of a whole theater are stacked on the sand: pallets, fuel bladders, replacement drafts waiting for the northbound flight. He processes through and moves up to Quang Tri Province and the fortified line below the Demilitarized Zone. He will pass through this airfield again, once outbound at the end of the tour and once inbound in 1970, the second time to appear as a witness rather than to join a unit.
suggested_refs: Marine Corps unit deployment histories for the northern I Corps, 1968-1969

stops.name: Cam Lo, the platoon below the DMZ
stops.date_confidence: attested to the tour (1968-1969) and to the decorations; the day given is a placeholder, since precise engagement dates rest on unit after-action reports not fully public
stops.campa: In Quang Tri Province, near Cam Lo, Second Lieutenant North commands a rifle platoon against North Vietnamese regulars along the line south of the Demilitarized Zone. He is wounded. He is awarded the Silver Star for valor, the Bronze Star Medal with Combat V, and two Purple Hearts across the tour. His defenders will return to this ground for the next forty years. The citations are on file at Headquarters Marine Corps, and nothing established in Washington after 1986 amends them.
suggested_refs: Marine Corps decoration citations for the Silver Star and Bronze Star with Combat V
sources: US Marine Corps decoration citations; official biography circulated at the 1987 hearings

stops.name: Da Nang, the court-martial of Randall Herrod
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1970; month and day not established in the reachable record. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 16.0, 107.8, which falls in the mountains southwest of Hue; the court-martial convened at Da Nang
stops.campa: North flies back to South Vietnam in 1970, not to a unit but to a courtroom, to testify at the court-martial of Lance Corporal Randall Herrod. He speaks for a Marine who had once fought beside him. He is not compelled to appear and he appears in uniform. The court-martial record is not public, and Wikipedia carries the episode alone, with no docket to check it against. Seventeen years later the tribunal will be televised and the loyalty in question will be his own.
suggested_refs: Court-martial record, United States v. Herrod, Da Nang, 1970

stops.name: Camp Gonsalves, the Northern Training Area
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1973-1974 (Wikipedia's Camp Gonsalves article lists Captain Oliver L. North among its commanders); month conventional. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 26.3344, 127.8056, central Okinawa near Kadena, roughly 55 km from the training area itself
stops.campa: North is director of the Northern Training Area on Okinawa, the jungle warfare school at Camp Gonsalves straddling Kunigami and Higashi in the far north of the island, where Marines are taught to move and fight in terrain built to resemble the one the Corps has just left. He runs the school for roughly a year, from 1973 to 1974. It is the last unit he commands. Every assignment after Okinawa is a staff billet, at Headquarters, at a battalion desk, and finally at the National Security Council.
suggested_refs: Jungle Warfare Training Center, Camp Gonsalves, commander rolls 1973-1974

stops.name: Camp Lejeune, operations officer of the 3rd Battalion
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1978-1980; month conventional. The preceding Marine Corps Headquarters tour is attested to 1975
stops.campa: North is operations officer of the 3rd Battalion, 8th Marine Regiment, 2nd Marine Division at Camp Lejeune, planning the movement of a battalion on paper before it moves on ground. Before this he has served as a plans and policy analyst at Marine Corps Headquarters in Washington, his first sustained exposure to the capital as a working machine rather than an address. Neither assignment involves troops in the field. Both involve the movement of paper between offices, which is the work he does for the next twenty years.
suggested_refs: 3rd Battalion, 8th Marines command chronologies, 1978-1980

stops.name: Newport, the College of Naval Command and Staff
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1981 graduation; month conventional. Contradiction flagged: the research pool's geography lens dated the Newport posting c.1978-1979, which cannot stand against the attested Camp Lejeune tour of 1978-1980 and the attested 1981 graduation. Both readings are recorded; the 1981 graduation is the documented one
stops.campa: North graduates from the College of Naval Command and Staff at the Naval War College in Newport, the professional schooling that separates the officers who will command from the officers who will staff the Pentagon and the White House. He is thirty-seven. Within months of leaving Newport he is assigned to the National Security Council, a White House staff, and he holds no Marine billet again. He remains a serving officer throughout, drawing Marine pay and wearing the uniform, while reporting to civilians outside the Corps.
suggested_refs: Naval War College, College of Naval Command and Staff, class of 1981

stops.name: The Old Executive Office Building, the desk beside the White House
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1981; month conventional. The promotion to lieutenant colonel and the appointment as deputy director for political-military affairs are attested to 1983
stops.campa: North joins the National Security Council staff in 1981, taking an office in the Old Executive Office Building beside the White House, at first in a liaison and lobbying role. He is promoted lieutenant colonel in 1983 and becomes deputy director for political-military affairs. From this desk, under National Security Advisers Robert McFarlane and then John Poindexter, and with the encouragement of CIA Director William Casey, he runs both the Contra resupply and the Iranian arms channel. The chain of authorization above him is never established by any of the three investigations.
suggested_refs: Room assignments and staff rosters of the National Security Council, 1981-1986
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: The Capitol, the second Boland Amendment
stops.date_confidence: attested: the second Boland Amendment takes effect in October 1984
stops.campa: Congress passes the second Boland Amendment, effective October 1984, barring United States intelligence and defense agencies from spending funds to support the Nicaraguan Contras. The National Security Council is not named in it. North and his superiors read the omission as permission. What follows is an operation of private donors, foreign governments, retired officers, and Swiss accounts, which its own participants call the Enterprise. The joint committees will spend 1987 establishing what the amendment did and did not cover.
suggested_refs: Text of the Boland Amendments, 1982-1986, and the congressional debate on their reach
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: The White House Situation Room, the PROF notes
stops.date_confidence: marker date for a practice attested across 1981-1986. The sources do not consistently distinguish which meetings occurred physically in the Situation Room complex and which in North's own office
stops.campa: North coordinates the apparatus by secure cable and by PROF notes, the White House internal messaging system, from the Situation Room complex and from his own office: CIA officers, Israeli intermediaries, Contra commanders in Honduras, arms brokers in three countries. He believes the messages are deleted when he deletes them. They are not. Recovered from backup tapes, the PROF notes will become the documentary spine of the congressional investigation and then of the government's case against him.
suggested_refs: The recovered PROF notes, entered as evidence in United States v. North
sources: Recovered PROF notes entered as evidence in US v. North

stops.name: Opa-locka, the airfield of the private airline
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1984-1986; the frequency and dates of North's individual Miami trips are inconsistently recorded across the sources
stops.campa: Opa-locka Airport north of Miami is where the Enterprise keeps its air arm: private pilots, retired military contractors, Cuban exile veterans who have been flying other men's cargo out of south Florida for a generation. Aircraft are loaded here for Central America. Congressional investigators will trace flight manifests and company records back to Miami front operations tied to Richard Secord and to North's office. North's coordinating visits are attested in trial testimony; a complete itinerary is not in the record.
suggested_refs: Flight manifests and corporate filings of the Miami-registered resupply companies
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Ilopango, the resupply base
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period; the pin is inherited byte-identical from the Ilopango stop in manuel_noriega.journey.json. North's personal presence at the field is reported by network associates and not confirmed by independent flight logs, and is [R]
stops.campa: Ilopango Air Base outside San Salvador is the far end of the pipeline: American-loaded aircraft land, refuel, and go on to airdrop over Nicaragua, with Salvadoran and American personnel on the field who know what the aircraft are carrying. Manuel Noriega's Panama supplies transit and deniability at the other side of the isthmus. North and William Casey run this end from Washington, which is how the Kerry Committee will describe it in 1988, and how the atlas already records it from Noriega's side.
suggested_refs: Kerry Committee report on the Contra resupply pipeline (1988)
sources: Eugene Hasenfus statements and Nicaraguan trial testimony, 1986
Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Tegucigalpa, the capital that denies the camps
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1984-1986; no complete itinerary of North's Honduran travel survives in the reachable record
stops.campa: Tegucigalpa is where the Contra war is administered: American military advisers, the CIA station, and Contra leadership meeting in a capital whose government publicly denies the base camps along its Nicaraguan border and privately permits them. North comes here to coordinate. The congressional hearings and the period reporting describe his visits without dating most of them. The airstrip at Aguacate, built with American assistance, feeds the same chain a hundred and fifty kilometres to the northeast.
suggested_refs: The Aguacate airstrip, Honduras, and the border base camps of the Contra forces
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Santa Elena, the airstrip on the Guanacaste coast
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1985 for the construction; whether North visited personally is not settled. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 10.95, -85.6167, some 20 to 25 km inland; the Santa Elena peninsula lies on the northwest Guanacaste coast
stops.campa: On the Guanacaste coast of northern Costa Rica, financed through the North-Secord network and disguised as a private ranching operation, a clandestine airstrip is built in 1985 to serve the southern front of the Contra war. Costa Rica has no army and a declared neutrality, and its officials are not told. When the strip surfaces in the investigation it becomes a national scandal there. President Oscar Arias, who resisted the pressure and wrote a regional peace plan instead, takes the Nobel Peace Prize in 1987.
suggested_refs: The Santa Elena strip, later within Santa Rosa National Park; La Nacion (Costa Rica) reporting, 1986-1987
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Geneva, the Lake Resources account
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1985-1986 for the account and the diversion; whether North personally traveled to Geneva or directed the account by cable and telephone is not settled and is [R]
stops.campa: Proceeds from the Iranian arms sales pass through a Credit Suisse account in Geneva held by Lake Resources, a shell corporation of the Enterprise controlled by Richard Secord and Albert Hakim, and a portion is turned toward the Contras. This is the diversion: the single fact that converts two separate covert operations into one crime. The research pool called Lake Resources a CIA proprietary front. It was not one, and the correction is recorded here rather than carried forward into the story.
suggested_refs: Financial appendices of the congressional Iran-Contra report tracing the Enterprise accounts
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)
Lawrence E. Walsh, Final Report of the Independent Counsel (1993)

stops.name: Leadenhall Street, the head office
stops.date_confidence: attested for the bank and the Kerry Committee findings; the pin is inherited byte-identical from the Leadenhall Street stops in manuel_noriega.journey.json and clark_clifford.journey.json. North's own transactions through BCCI are not individually documented in the reachable record and the association is [R]
stops.campa: The head office of the Bank of Credit and Commerce International stands on Leadenhall Street, and from it Agha Hasan Abedi's correspondent network reaches everywhere else, including the Panama branch that holds Manuel Noriega's accounts. The Senate's Kerry Committee ties the same institution to Iran-Contra financing in 1992, four years after tying the Contra pipeline to Ilopango. Mark Lombardi draws the whole thing as arcs on paper: Abedi, Clark Clifford, North, Casey, Noriega, one diagram, no words.
suggested_refs: Mark Lombardi's BCCI network drawings; US Senate Kerry Committee report on BCCI (1992)
sources: US Senate Kerry Committee report on BCCI (1992)

stops.name: Tel Aviv, the intermediary
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1985-1986 for the meetings; the exact dates of individual trips vary between North's testimony and the Israeli sources, and the Tower Commission does not reconcile them
stops.campa: North travels repeatedly to Tel Aviv in 1985 and 1986 to meet Amiram Nir, counterterrorism adviser to the Israeli prime minister, and the officials running the arms channel to Iran. Israel is supplier and go-between at once, shipping American-origin missiles to Tehran with Washington's approval before United States stocks are drawn on directly. On paper the missiles leave an Israeli port under an Israeli manifest, which is what allows Washington to deny them. North's testimony and the Israeli accounts disagree over the dates of individual trips, and the Tower Commission does not reconcile them.
suggested_refs: Israeli and American press accounts of the Nir channel, 1985-1987

stops.name: Sigonella, the airliner forced down
stops.date_confidence: attested: the interception occurred on 10 October 1985. Tag corrected from [R] to [A]: Wikipedia's account of the Achille Lauro hijacking documents North's role directly rather than reporting it at second hand
stops.campa: After the hijacking of the cruise ship Achille Lauro, North and Commander James Stark originate the idea of intercepting the Egyptian airliner carrying the hijackers out. North contacts the Israeli Major General Uri Simhoni for the flight details, and the two pass the plan to John Poindexter. On the tenth of October Navy fighters force the airliner down at the naval air station at Sigonella. It is the one operation of North's tenure on the National Security Council staff that the administration claims publicly at the time.
suggested_refs: Naval Air Station Sigonella, Sicily, and the standoff on the runway between American and Italian forces

stops.name: London, the broker Ghorbanifar
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1985-1986; no single hotel is consistently named across the sources and the month given is representative
stops.campa: In London hotel rooms in 1985 and 1986 North meets Manucher Ghorbanifar, the Iranian broker who is the channel's indispensable and least trustworthy component, and negotiates prices, quantities, and shipment schedules. London is neutral ground for a transaction too sensitive for either capital. Ghorbanifar's later account to investigators conflicts with North's over what was promised and to whom. Neither version is confirmed by the other, and the congressional report sets them side by side without choosing.
suggested_refs: Ghorbanifar's statements to congressional investigators and the independent counsel
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Tehran, the cake and the inscribed Bible
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 May 1986. The pin is inherited byte-identical from the Tehran pins in ayatollah_khomeini.journey.json and the interlock record; the delegation in fact landed at Mehrabad, some five kilometres west of this point
stops.campa: Robert McFarlane, no longer National Security Adviser, flies into Tehran with North and a small delegation, carrying a Bible inscribed by Reagan, missile spare parts, and a cake shaped like a key. They expect the Iranian leadership. They are received by mid-level officials, kept waiting, and sent home with no hostages. The counterparty is Ayatollah Khomeini's republic, which took the American embassy here in 1979 after Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi fell. The hostages being traded for are held in Beirut.
suggested_refs: The inscribed Bible and the key-shaped cake, the two objects by which the mission is remembered

stops.name: Frankfurt, the second channel
stops.date_confidence: attested: the congressional report documents Frankfurt meetings in February 1986 and again in October 1986. Tag corrected from [R] to [A]; the research pool's hedge that other chronologies place these meetings elsewhere in Europe is dropped as unsupported
stops.campa: Frankfurt serves the channel twice: a meeting in February 1986 and another in October, the second being where the Iranian Second Channel is opened after Ghorbanifar's line has soured. It is a convenient hub for men traveling from Washington, Tel Aviv, and Tehran on separate passports. By the time of the October meeting a cargo aircraft has already come down over Nicaragua, and the Beirut magazine that will print the other half of the story is a month from going to press.
suggested_refs: The October 1986 Frankfurt meeting at which the Second Channel was opened
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Southern Nicaragua, the plane comes down
stops.date_confidence: attested to 5 October 1986; the coordinates are approximate for southern Nicaragua rather than a surveyed crash site
stops.campa: A cargo aircraft carrying weapons and supplies to Contra forces is shot down over southern Nicaragua. The crewman Eugene Hasenfus survives, is captured, and tells the Sandinistas and then a Nicaraguan court that he was flying for an American covert operation. The Enterprise has run for two years without a public trace. Hasenfus is the trace, and he is in Sandinista custody with a lawyer and a press corps. The research pool credited the exposure to his congressional testimony; that came later, and the correction is recorded here.
suggested_refs: The Hasenfus aircraft wreckage and the Nicaraguan trial record, October to December 1986
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: Beirut, Ash-Shiraa prints the other half
stops.date_confidence: attested to 3 November 1986
stops.campa: The Lebanese magazine Ash-Shiraa prints the first public account of the other half: that the United States has been secretly selling weapons to Iran, and that Robert McFarlane came to Tehran in person to do it. The report runs on the third of November in a city where the American hostages the deal was meant to buy back are still held. Within three weeks the two halves will be joined in one sentence spoken by the Attorney General of the United States, and the phrase Iran-Contra will exist.
suggested_refs: Ash-Shiraa, Beirut, issue of 3 November 1986
sources: Report of the Congressional Committees Investigating the Iran-Contra Affair (1987)

stops.name: The Old Executive Office Building, the shredder
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1986; the specific days on which documents were shredded and altered are given variously across the testimony and are not fixed here
stops.campa: In the days after the story breaks, North and his secretary Fawn Hall work the shredder in the Old Executive Office Building, destroying and altering National Security Council documents on the Iran sales and the Contra diversion. Hall carries further papers out of the building concealed in her clothing. The PROF notes they believe deleted are held on backup tapes in the same building. Investigators will recover them within the year and read them into the congressional record.
suggested_refs: Fawn Hall's congressional testimony, June 1987, on the shredding and removal of documents

stops.name: The White House, the dismissal announced
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 November 1986. The research pool placed the announcement at a Rose Garden press conference; it was made in the White House press briefing room, and since neither the Reagan Library nor the American Presidency Project copy of the transcript was reachable, the venue is stated here only as the White House
stops.campa: Attorney General Edwin Meese tells the White House press room that profits from the Iran arms sales were diverted to the Contras. Reagan reads a short statement and hands Meese the questions. North is dismissed from the National Security Council the same day and John Poindexter resigns. Six months later, on the sixth of May 1987, William Casey, who had encouraged the operation, dies of a brain tumour at Glen Cove. He is never deposed, and no investigation establishes what he authorized or when.
stops.quote: I'm trusting in the Lord and a good lawyer.
stops.quote_source: Oliver North, quoted in Tom Morganthau, "Trusting 'in the Lord and a Good Lawyer,'" Newsweek, 8 December 1986, pp. 46-47
suggested_refs: The White House press briefing of 25 November 1986; the grave of William Casey, Glen Cove, New York
sources: Contemporaneous New York Times and Washington Post reporting

stops.name: The Russell Senate Office Building, Fawn Hall before the committees
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1987; the day is not fixed here. The hearings sat in the Senate Caucus Room of the Russell Senate Office Building and in the Rayburn House Office Building, not in the Capitol, and the pin is corrected accordingly
stops.campa: Fawn Hall testifies before the joint congressional committees about shredding National Security Council documents and about carrying others out of the building concealed in her clothing. She is granted immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony against her former superior. The immunity order covers her account of the documents and nothing else. She is in her twenties, and for one season she is famous. Thirty-eight years later, after the death of North's wife, she will marry him.
suggested_refs: The Senate Caucus Room of the Russell Senate Office Building, seat of the joint committees
sources: Official transcript, Iran-Contra congressional hearings, June 1987

stops.name: The Russell Senate Office Building, the first day of testimony
stops.date_confidence: attested: testimony ran 7 to 14 July 1987
stops.campa: North takes the witness table in Marine dress uniform, ribbons visible, and begins six days of testimony under a grant of limited immunity. House counsel John Nields questions him first. He concedes that he misled Congress, that he shredded documents, that he wrote false chronologies. He does not concede that he acted alone or wrongly. The sessions run live on the networks, the supportive mail arrives at the committees by the sack, and the merchandise is on sale within the week.
stops.quote: I was authorized to do everything that I did.
stops.quote_source: Oliver North to House counsel John Nields, testimony before the Joint House-Senate Iran-Contra Committee, 7 July 1987; verbatim transcript printed in Taking the Stand: The Testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Oliver L. North (Pocket Books, 1987). The research pool dated this to 8 July; the correction to 7 July is carried here
suggested_refs: C-SPAN broadcast archive of the Iran-Contra hearings, July 1987
sources: Official transcript, Iran-Contra congressional hearings, July 1987

stops.name: The Russell Senate Office Building, the sixth day
stops.date_confidence: attested: the final day of North's testimony
stops.campa: The testimony runs from the seventh to the fourteenth of July. By the sixth day counsel are reading documents into the record and the witness is answering in the register of a man reporting to a superior officer. Senator Warren Rudman reads North's own claim of the first day back to him: he has never in twenty-three years violated an order. The question is which order. North names Reagan's policy, McFarlane, Poindexter, and Casey. Of that chain, one is dead, two have resigned, and the fourth is not called.
stops.quote: I never carried out a single act, not one, Mr. Nields, in which I did not have authority from my superiors. I haven't in the 23 years that I have been in the uniformed Services of the United States of America ever violated an order, not one.
stops.quote_source: Oliver North to House counsel John Nields, 7 July 1987, read back to him by Senator Warren Rudman on 14 July 1987; verbatim transcript in Taking the Stand (Pocket Books, 1987). The research pool dated the utterance to 8 July; the correction to 7 July is carried here
suggested_refs: Taking the Stand: The Testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Oliver L. North (Pocket Books, 1987)
sources: Official transcript, Iran-Contra congressional hearings, July 1987

stops.name: The E. Barrett Prettyman Courthouse, twelve counts of sixteen
stops.date_confidence: attested: the indictment was returned 16 March 1988 and the jury sworn 21 February 1989 (Walsh, Final Report). Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 38.8977, -77.0365, which is the White House
stops.campa: A federal grand jury indicts North on sixteen felony counts alongside John Poindexter, Richard Secord, and Albert Hakim. The case erodes before it reaches a jury. One wire-fraud count is dismissed in November 1988 as duplicative, and on the thirteenth of January 1989 the conspiracy and theft counts go when the administration refuses to declassify the material the trial would require. Twelve counts remain when the jury is sworn on the twenty-first of February, before Judge Gerhard Gesell.
suggested_refs: United States v. North docket, US District Court for the District of Columbia
sources: Walsh, Final Report of the Independent Counsel (1993), ch. 2

stops.name: The E. Barrett Prettyman Courthouse, three counts of twelve
stops.date_confidence: attested to 4 May 1989 for the verdict and 5 July 1989 for the sentence. The research pool's claim that the jury deadlocked on remaining charges is false and is corrected here: three guilty and nine not guilty account for all twelve counts
stops.campa: The jury convicts North on three counts: obstructing a congressional inquiry, destroying documents, and accepting an illegal gratuity, a security system installed at his house at another man's expense. It acquits him on the other nine. Three and nine make twelve, and nothing hangs. In July, Judge Gesell suspends the prison term and imposes a fine, probation, and community service. The widely repeated account of a deadlocked jury and dropped charges has no basis in the docket.
suggested_refs: Verdict sheet and sentencing order, United States v. North, May and July 1989
sources: Walsh, Final Report of the Independent Counsel (1993), ch. 2
US v. North verdict reporting, 4 May 1989

stops.name: The E. Barrett Prettyman Courthouse, the convictions vacated
stops.date_confidence: attested to 20 July 1990. Coordinates corrected: the research pool gave 38.8951, -77.0364, near 17th Street NW by the Eisenhower Executive Office Building, roughly 1.9 km from any courthouse
stops.campa: The Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit vacates the convictions and remands, holding that North's immunized 1987 testimony may have tainted the witnesses who testified against him, and that the trial court did not adequately test whether it had. The ruling turns on Kastigar, a rule about the use of immunized testimony, and reaches no finding on whether North did the acts charged. Popular retelling flattens it into the sentence that Oliver North was exonerated. The opinion does not contain that word or any finding of innocence.
suggested_refs: United States v. North, 910 F.2d 843 (D.C. Cir. 1990)
sources: United States v. North, 910 F.2d 843 (D.C. Cir. 1990)

stops.name: The E. Barrett Prettyman Courthouse, the charges dismissed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 September 1991
stops.campa: Judge Gesell dismisses the remaining charges after the independent counsel concludes that the taint from the immunized testimony cannot be overcome and moves to end the case. There is no retrial and no acquittal. The matter closes in the building where it opened, with a docket entry rather than a verdict, and Lawrence Walsh's final report of 1993 sets down what the prosecution believed it could once have proved. North leaves the case with no convictions on his record and no acquittal on the merits.
